lead: The Furnas suture technique is an otoplasty (ear surgery) method that sets back a prominent ear by placing permanent or long-lasting sutures between the conchal cartilage (the bowl of the ear) and the mastoid periosteum behind the ear. It was described by David Furnas in 1968 and is often paired with the Mustardé technique, which forms the antihelical fold with mattress sutures [1][3]. People who choose it want ears that sit closer to the head, which changes the silhouette of the face from the front and the side.

It addresses ears whose prominence comes mainly from a deep or wide concha. Because it leaves the cartilage uncut, it belongs to the group of cartilage-sparing otoplasty methods [1][3]. In looksmaxxing discussions it is classed as a surgical (hardmaxx) option for the ears.

Published work consists of surgical technique papers and case series. A 2025 overview describes the preparation, surgical steps, postoperative care and complications of Mustardé and Furnas otoplasty [3], and other surgeons report that these suture methods can recur because of cartilage memory and suture fatigue [4]. Prominent ears are described as affecting about 5 percent of the population and as being associated with emotional stress and social restrictions in the surgical literature [5].

paras: In the Furnas approach, sutures anchor the back of the concha to the mastoid fascia or periosteum, reducing the angle between the ear and the head (the cephaloauricular angle) [1][2]. Wikipedia lists it among the suture-only techniques in which the cartilage stays intact, and describes the underlying problem as a deep or wide concha, an underdeveloped antihelical fold, or a protruding lobule [1].

Surgeons commonly combine it with Mustardé sutures, which recreate the antihelix, so that both the fold and the conchal depth are addressed in one operation [2][3]. Otoplasty techniques fall into groups: suture-only methods that leave cartilage intact (such as Mustardé, the Merck stitch method and incisionless Fritsch otoplasty), cartilage-cutting methods (such as Converse and Chongchet-Stenström) and excision methods; Furnas is described as the concha-to-mastoid suture method within the suture-only group [1].

The Sushruta Samhita, around 500 AD, describes ear surgery in ancient India, and Dieffenbach described the first surgery for prominent ears in 1845, including suturing the ear to the mastoid periosteum [1]. Edward Talbott Ely performed an early elective ear pinback in 1881 [1]. Mustardé published his suture technique in 1963 and Stenström described his in the same period; Furnas published conchomastoid suturing in 1968 [1][2].

Wikipedia notes that more than 170 otoplasty procedures have been developed [1]. The move toward suture-based cartilage-sparing methods has been attributed in part to concern about haematoma, skin necrosis and deformity with cartilage-cutting techniques [4].

Otoplasty may be done as an outpatient or in hospital and can take about 1.5 to 5 hours; local anaesthesia, local with sedation, or general anaesthesia are used, and general anaesthesia is usual for children [1]. Children with very prominent ears can have surgery around age 4 [1]. A loose, non-compressive dressing is worn for several days, bruising and swelling usually fade within about two weeks, and a snug headband is worn during sleep for roughly 3 to 6 weeks to keep the ears from folding forward [1].

Reported drawbacks of suture-only methods include recurrence of the deformity through cartilage memory and suture fatigue, and suture extrusion [4][5]. Surgeons have described adding a postauricular dermal flap, either laterally or medially based, to reduce suture extrusion and recurrence [4][5]. Grokipedia gives recurrence of prominence at 3 to 10 percent across otoplasty generally and suture extrusion around 2.5 percent, though its citations are not all specific to this technique [2].

Wikipedia lists hematoma, infection, suture extrusion and overcorrection among otoplasty complications, with suture extrusion the most common; infection is rare but must be treated quickly to prevent chondritis, and overcorrection produces an unnatural contour [1].

Evidence is mostly retrospective surgical series. A 2016 series of 47 patients (41 bilateral, 6 unilateral; mean age 14.5 years) combined Mustardé and Furnas sutures with a laterally based postauricular dermal flap fixed to the mastoid. At 12 months the helix-mastoid distance was about 16.3 mm and the concha-mastoid angle about 25.7 degrees, with changes of 1 to 3 mm and 1 to 2 degrees from earlier time points, and the authors described the method as effective for preventing suture extrusion and recurrence [5].

A 2023 report of 34 patients (14 female, 20 male) used a medially based perichondrio-adipo-dermal flap in cartilage-sparing surgery. Operative time averaged 80 minutes; one patient had a haematoma, one a small area of necrosis on the new fold, and deformity recurred in one patient (about 2.9 percent), with no suture extrusion reported [4].

One report of 17 children with prominent lobules combined antitragicus muscle resection and helical tail setback with a Mustardé or Furnas suture technique, and the authors state all had satisfactory outcomes [6]. A 2025 review in Facial Plastic Surgery summarizes technique and complications [3]. No randomized trials have been published.

name: Furnas suture technique

card.summary: Concha-to-mastoid stitches that pin back a deep ear bowl; an established surgical technique with case-series evidence and a known recurrence risk.
card.note: Suture extrusion and recurrence are reported; surgeon-performed only.

quick.overview:
The Furnas technique is an ear-pinning method that sutures the concha to the bone-covering tissue behind the ear to bring a protruding ear closer to the head. It leaves the cartilage uncut and is often combined with Mustardé sutures.
It is a long-established otoplasty approach documented in surgical case series, mainly for prominent ears in children and adults.
quick.mechanism: Stitches anchor the back of the conchal bowl to the mastoid periosteum, reducing the ear-to-head angle without cutting cartilage.
quick.risks: Reported complications include hematoma, infection, suture extrusion, overcorrection and recurrence from suture fatigue or cartilage memory. Surgeons have described flaps to reduce extrusion and recurrence.
